results.whats_broken: VLOOKUP returns #N/A for about half the rows even though the codes appear to exist in the price list.
results.why: VLOOKUP compares values exactly, so if the code in column A is stored as text (for example '00123') while the price list stores it as a number (123), or if there are hidden spaces, the match fails. Another common cause is that the codes are not in column A of the 'Price List' sheet, since VLOOKUP can only search the first column of the range.
results.what_changed: Wrapped the lookup value in TRIM to remove stray spaces and added IFERROR so unmatched rows show a blank instead of #N/A; if the codes are numbers stored as text, use VALUE($A2) or TEXT($A2,"0") to match the price list format.

results.whats_broken: The lookup value in D2 is stored as text (green triangle warning) while the IDs in Orders!B2:B5000 are stored as numbers, so XLOOKUP finds no match.
results.why: The green triangles in Excel mean the cells contain numbers saved as text. XLOOKUP compares values strictly, so the text "12345" does not equal the number 12345, and it returns #N/A for every row. This is a data-type mismatch, not a formula error.
results.what_changed: Wrapped the lookup value in VALUE(TRIM(...)) to convert the text ID to a number before matching. If the Orders sheet IDs are also text, use =XLOOKUP(TRIM(D2),Orders!$B$2:$B$5000,Orders!$F$2:$F$5000) instead.

results.whats_broken: The last argument TRUE makes VLOOKUP do an approximate match, which is wrong for looking up a client's name.
results.why: VLOOKUP's fourth argument controls the match type: TRUE means 'find the closest value that is not greater than the lookup value', which only makes sense for sorted numeric ranges. For text like surnames it returns a random nearby name's price (the 'чужая цена' problem) and gives #N/A when the name sorts before the first entry. You need an exact match, which is FALSE (or 0).
results.what_changed: Changed the fourth argument from TRUE to FALSE so VLOOKUP requires an exact surname match instead of an approximate one.
results.if_ok_suggestion: If you have Excel 365 or 2021, use =XLOOKUP(E2,$A$2:$A$200,$B$2:$B$200,"не найдено") — it looks up exactly by default, returns a friendly message instead of #N/A, and doesn't need column numbers.

results.whats_broken: The VLOOKUP returns #N/A for rows where the lookup value in column A doesn't exist in the reference sheet.
results.why: VLOOKUP looks for each value from A2:A inside Ref!A2:B300 and returns the matching value from column B. When a value isn't found (or has extra spaces, different case, or is a number stored as text), VLOOKUP shows #N/A. Because ARRAYFORMULA applies this to the whole column, every unmatched row shows #N/A, which is why you see a solid block of them at the bottom.
results.what_changed: Wrapped the VLOOKUP in IFERROR so missing matches show blank instead of #N/A, and added an IF to skip empty rows.

results.whats_broken: MATCH can't find today's date in the header row, even though it looks like it's there.
results.why: The most likely cause is that the dates in B1:AF1 are not real dates but text (for example, typed with a leading apostrophe or formatted as Text), so Excel compares text against the real date returned by TODAY() and finds no match. Another common cause is that the header contains a full date-time (with a hidden time part) while TODAY() is midnight, so the values are not exactly equal. A third possibility is that the header dates are in a different year or month than today.
results.what_changed: Wraps the header range in DATEVALUE(TEXT(...,"yyyy-mm-dd")) so text dates are converted to real dates before matching; if the header contains date-times, use =MATCH(TODAY(),INDEX(INT($B$1:$AF$1),0),0) instead.
